summary: Describes an experimental policy for using the 233/8 block of the multicast address space as a statically assigned set, with addresses derived from autonomous system numbers. It is an experimental protocol, and it was replaced by RFC 3180.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2770 proposes deriving a block of static multicast addresses from each network's registered Autonomous System number. It is an experimental specification, later replaced by RFC 3180.

questions: how are multicast addresses assigned in 233/8
how does an as number produce a multicast address
subtitle: An experimental way to assign static multicast addresses using an AS number

tldr.problem: Some multicast applications need group addresses that stay fixed, while dynamic allocation approaches were not suitable or agreed upon for every use.
tldr.mechanism: The experiment uses the 233/8 block and places an existing 16-bit Autonomous System number in the next 16 bits, leaving the remaining bits for local use.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines an experimental allocation with a one-year timeout, and was later replaced by RFC 3180.

today: RFC 2770 is Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 3180.

sections.title: Why Use Static Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
Multicast addresses identify groups that can receive the same traffic. The RFC says some applications need addresses to remain fixed, while dynamic allocation may not fit those models. It also notes a lack of general agreement among providers, content aggregators and application writers about allocation mechanisms.

This document proposes an experimental method for static allocation with global scope, alongside other allocation approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Some group-address users need to know an address in advance and keep it fixed. This RFC proposes a way to assign such addresses without requesting one dynamically each time.

sections.title: Deriving an Address from an AS Number
sections.content:
The IANA allocated 233/8 for this experiment. The address begins with 233, followed by the 16-bit Autonomous System number split across two octets; the remaining 8 bits are local bits. The RFC's example maps AS 5662 to 233.22.30/24.

Each AS receives one /24 block. Because the AS number is already assigned and registered, this method does not require an additional registration step. Address space corresponding to private AS numbers is reserved for future allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: The first part of each address identifies the experiment, and the next part comes from the network's AS number. The remaining part is available for local assignment within that block.

sections.title: Trial Period and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says the experimental assignment should time out one year after it is made, though it may be renewed. Static addresses could serve applications that need them, while the document also describes dynamic allocation, administratively scoped addresses and single-source addresses as other possibilities.

For security, it says this approach may reduce exposure to denial-of-space attacks based on dynamic allocation. Before using experimental values across networks outside an experimenter's full control, the RFC says possible harmful side effects need careful evaluation.
sections.plainLanguage: The allocation was temporary unless renewed. The RFC also warns that people should evaluate possible harm before using experimental addresses across networks they do not fully control.
